conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I've been reviewing your case. You were admitted this morning with increased bowel movements and left abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thanks. It started about six days ago—more frequent stools, but still soft, like my usual. Then two days ago, it got worse—watery every 20 minutes until 3 AM yesterday. Then nothing until this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the pain—where is it located?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Left lower abdomen. Dull at first, then sharp. It eases a bit after I go to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bright red blood. Some black color, but that’s normal for me—probably from the iron supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you mentioned back pain too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, left lower back. There’s a bump there I’ve had for months. It’s been sharper lately, burning sometimes. Hurts more when I breathe or move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did the morphine in the ER help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for about 20 minutes. Felt like my old kidney stone pain, but no burning when I pee or blood in urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We’ve run some tests. Your stool came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and parasites. So it doesn’t look like an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my Crohn’s acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we suspect. Your white blood cell count is a bit high, and you have a mild acidosis—likely from dehydration due to the diarrhea. We’re giving you IV fluids and starting IV steroids to calm the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was trying to taper down my prednisone—down to 20 mg. But when things got worse, I bumped it back to 40 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was a reasonable step. But since you’re having a flare, we’re switching to IV steroids for better control. We’ll transition back to oral later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the back pain? I’m worried it’s something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. Given your steroid use and the nature of the pain, we’re concerned about possible avascular necrosis or an abscess. We’ve ordered MRIs of your spine and hips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids can cause that? I didn’t know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, long-term use increases the risk. But we’ll know more after the scans. For now, we’re monitoring you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I have updates on your imaging. The abdominal X-ray showed no obstruction or free air. The MRI of your abdomen shows active Crohn’s inflammation in your distal ileum—same area as before—and a new inflamed segment nearby.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely a flare. Is the new area serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but not an emergency. No abscess or fistula. We’ll continue IV steroids and monitor your response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the back and hip MRIs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—no avascular necrosis in the hips and no spinal abscess. Just some degenerative disc changes, which are stable. Your pain may be musculoskeletal, possibly aggravated by posture or strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So no surgery needed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. We’re focusing on controlling the Crohn’s flare medically. You’ve also been smoking more—any reason?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stress. I know it’s not helping, but it’s hard to quit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smoking can worsen Crohn’s. We can connect you with counseling and support to quit. It would help your long-term outcomes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d appreciate that. I want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. Your bowel movements have slowed, and your pain is less severe. Labs show your acidosis is improving with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Can I start eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids and advance slowly. We don’t want to overwhelm your bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about the steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to oral prednisone tomorrow—start at 40 mg, then taper slowly with your gastroenterologist. Rapid tapering can trigger flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I learned that the hard way. What about my B12 and other deficiencies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re due for a B12 injection before discharge. We also noted a B-complex deficiency—we’ll send you home with a supplement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my eyes? I’ve been meaning to get my cataracts checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve noted the cataracts. They’re not urgent, but you should follow up with your ophthalmologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the kidney cysts? The MRI mentioned them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Small, bilateral cysts—very common, especially with age. No action needed unless they grow or cause symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I worry about every little thing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. You’ve been through a lot with your Crohn’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’d like to discharge you today. You’ve been off IVs, eating without issues, and your pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What’s the plan after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue prednisone 40 mg daily, then taper as directed by your GI doctor. Take the B-complex supplement, stay on B12 injections, and avoid NSAIDs—they’re on your allergy list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know—no ibuprofen. What about pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use acetaminophen if needed. Avoid narcotics unless absolutely necessary. And please follow up with smoking cessation—we’ve added a referral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if diarrhea returns, pain worsens, or you develop fever. Otherwise, see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take it one day at a time.
